newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Britain open new aviation talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Britain open new aviation talks.

text.p: The United States and Britain are to start yet another attempt on Wednesday to reach an aviation accord that would end restrictions on airline traffic between the two countries.
Past efforts have ended in failure, most recently in August when the United States cancelled talks then under way, citing lack of progress. Washington requested a resumption of talks, officials said.
U.S. officials called the talks on Wednesday and Thursday preliminary and said they would enter a more advanced stage later this month in London but only if progress was made.

A so-called "open skies" accord would give U.S. and British airlines the right to fly into any city in the other's country as often as they wish. Routes and flight frequencies between Britain and the United States are heavily regulated.

Access for U.S. carriers to London's Heathrow Airport has been a sticking point in previous talks and the U.S. officials made it clear that expanded Heathrow landing rights had to be part of any new aviation accord.

British Airways Plc (BA) controls 38 percent of landing slots at Heathrow -- considered a vital transfer point for service to continental Europe and beyond -- but has been reluctant to cede them to U.S. trans-Atlantic competitors.
The United States has said an "open skies" accord could not be reached without an opening of Heathrow.

"The U.S. goal remains acceptance of all essential elements of an 'open skies' regime in an operating environment that allows the available rights to be exercised effectively," one U.S. official said, referring to Heathrow.
Also at stake in the talks is the future of planned trans-Atlantic alliance between British Airways and American Airlines.
Officials in Washington have said government immunity from antitrust laws would not be granted to American, the nation's second-largest carrier, unless an "open skies" accord was first reached.

Other U.S. airlines that have marketing alliances with European carriers include United Airlines, the nation's largest airline, with Deutsche Lufthansa AG, and Northwest Airlines, with KLM Royal Dutch Airlines NV.
Those alliances, and the granting of antitrust immunity they required, came after the United States reached "open skies" agreements with Germany and the Netherlands.
U.S. officials gave no reason for initiating the new talks with Britain, but said they had remained in touch with their British counterparts since the last round of talks ended.
The talks this week would be "government-to-government," they said, with no industry representatives at the table.
If progress were made and full negotiations opened later this month, industry officials would be called in for their views on any U.S.-British accord.

In Geneva, Switzerland, a senior European Union official urged that ownership and control restrictions be dismantled in the airline industry with the final aim of bringing it under the global rules of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

Ludolf von Hasselt, a top airline official with the European Union's executive commission, said that without such progress, aviation would be left behind by the growing liberalisation of the world economy.
"Ownership and control restrictions are, in my view, the most important barrier against air carriers enlarging their scale and becoming global operators," he told industry executives.
The current exclusion of the industry from the mainstream of world trade rules in goods and services, he said, "will increasingly put aviation at a disadvantage."
